# Introduction to Ecclesiastes

## Outline of Ecclesiastes

1. The author questions the nature of life and the limits of human wisdom (1:1–6:12).
2. The author teaches about making wise choices in how one lives (7:1–12:7)
3. The conclusion and ending (12:8–14)

### What is the book of Ecclesiastes about?

Ecclesiastes is a group of short teachings that try to answer questions such as “What profit {belongs} to humanity in exchange for all his toil that he toils under the sun?” (1:3) Ecclesiastes is a series of thoughts about a variety of subjects, all of them about the purpose and worth of various actions and events. The author concludes that all the work we perform and all the knowledge and skill we gain are as a vapor that disappears, and that we must fear Yahweh and keep his commandments.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title for this book is “Ecclesiastes.” Its meaning is similar to “religious assembly.” Translators might use a different title such as “Words of a Teacher” or “Teachings of a Wise Man.”

### Who wrote the book of Ecclesiastes?

The writer calls himself Qoheleth and identifies himself as “the son of David, king in Jerusalem.” Jewish and Christian tradition identify Qoheleth with King Solomon based on:

* his wisdom (1:16 and twenty-six other references to wisdom)
* his vast wealth (2:8) and the pain that comes from wealth (4:8, 5:13–14, 9:11)
* his large number of servants (2:7 and 10:7)
* his limitless opportunities for worldly pleasures (2:1–2, 9, 3:13, 4:8, 5:4 and 12:1) and
* the wide range of his many building projects (2:4–6).

Some scholars think that Qoheleth was a later anonymous Jewish writer. He appears to have written the book of Ecclesiastes near the end of his life, as he reflected on what he gained from all that he did.

### Why are there so many apparent contradictions in the book of Ecclesiastes?

Some scholars think the author was a faithful man. Other scholars think that the author made bad decisions and was sorrowful when he wrote this book. Apparent contradictions in the book may indicate that Qoheleth’s faith was sometimes weak. Or it is also possible that the teachings in the book differ from each other in order to relate to different things happening in the lives of readers.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What does this book teach about how God repays people?

In the ancient Near East, people were concerned with why they were being punished or blessed. They often connected these things to their gods. The writer of Ecclesiastes explains that Yahweh will bless and reward people for the right things they do and punish people for the evil things they do. But this might not happen in this life.

### What value did the Israelites place on the book of Ecclesiastes?

The Israelites have often questioned the value of this book. This is due in large part to its unusual wording and teachings. At times, it appears to disagree with the rest of Scripture. While many have questioned its authority, it has been affirmed to be Scripture. It gives valuable lessons concerning the uselessness of pursuing any goal other than to give Yahweh glory.

### Vapor as Futility

The Hebrew word translated as “vapor” recurs as a thematic refrain throughout Ecclesiastes, declaring human achievements fleeting. It indicates transience, not moral worthlessness. The paired phrase “pursuit of wind” intensifies this assessment.

## Translation Issues

### What is the meaning of “under the sun?”

“Under the sun” here is another way of saying “on the earth.” When the author says that there is “nothing new under the sun,” this means that every kind of thing has already happened before on the earth. While a particular event may not have specifically occurred before, something similar has already occurred.
Translate this phrase consistently through the book.

### How do I translate harsh or shocking passages?

Parts of the book of Ecclesiastes can be shocking or surprising to read in Scripture. For example, “If a man should father a hundred {children}, and many years should he live—and many that the days of his years may be—but {if} his soul is not satisfied from the good {thing} (and also a burial place is not for him), I say, ‘Better than him {is} the stillborn child.’” (6:3). The translator should allow these difficulties to remain and not try to make them less surprising.

### How is life described in the book of Ecclesiastes?

The author of Ecclesiastes concludes that everything in this life quickly passes away, like a vapor that disappears. A person’s circumstances or character and even all of the things of this world have little or no significance apart from God. That is because God gives meaning to everything.

At the end of their life, people often say that the years of their life seemed short. The author of Ecclesiastes used the metaphor of vapor or breath to describe how life ends while it seems to be just beginning.

The word **Qoheleth** is the name that the main speaker of this book chose to use for himself. ## Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from instruction about worship and vows (1–7) to reflection on oppression and wealth (8–17), closing with counsel to enjoy God’s gifts (18–20).

### Vows

A person could promise God to do something in return for help. Such a promise was binding, so the writer warns against vowing rashly.

The writer calls things “vapor” (7, 10), a recurring image for what is fleeting and empty. See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for a further explanation of this term and its usage.

# Ecclesiastes 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Qheleth continues his examination of wealth and mortality, arguing that neither abundance nor long life benefits a person who is unable to enjoy them.

  1. Wealth that God gives but does not allow a person to enjoy (1–2)
  2. A long, unsatisfied life is worse than a stillborn child (3–6)
  3. Sayings about appetite, wisdom, and desire (7–9)
  4. Human limits before the one who is more powerful (10–12)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 6:7 and 6:9.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Vapor

The word rendered “vapor” recurs through this chapter (verses 2, 4, 9, 11, and 12) as the book’s key image for what is fleeting and insubstantial, not for what is morally worthless.

### Burial

In this culture a proper burial honored the dead, so the remark that “a burial place is not for him” (3) describes a disgrace rather than merely an absence.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Rhetorical Questions

The Teacher advances much of his argument by asking questions that expect no answer (verses 6, 8, 11, and 12). If questions do not work this way in your language, you could translate them as statements.

### Quoted Sayings

Verses 7 and 9 appear to be popular sayings that the Teacher quotes in support of his argument. If it would be helpful, you could mark them as quoted sayings.

# Ecclesiastes 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter first gathers proverbs about wisdom, mortality, and the limits of human understanding, and then records Qoheleth’s own search for understanding.

  1. Better-than proverbs about mourning, grief, and rebuke (1–6)
  2. Further proverbs about patience, anger, and the protection wisdom gives (7–12)
  3. A call to consider God’s work in good times and bad (13–14)
  4. Counsel about righteousness, wisdom, and human sinfulness (15–22)
  5. Qoheleth’s search for the scheme of things (23–29)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [7:1–12](../07/01.md), [7:14–18](../07/14.md), and [7:26–29](../07/26.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Better-than sayings

Many verses in this chapter use a proverb form that sets two things side by side and declares one of them more advantageous than the other. The comparison is practical rather than absolute: it commends what teaches a person about life, not what feels pleasant. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-proverbs]]; and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/proverb]])

### Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears again in this chapter in verses 6 and 15. Render it consistently through the book.

### Fearing God

In verse 18, the person who fears God is the person who reverently acknowledges God’s rule and lives accordingly. This is respectful submission, not terror. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/fear]])

### The heart

Throughout the chapter, “heart” stands for the inner person: thoughts, inclination, and moral judgment. If your readers would not understand this use of “heart,” consider a term in your language that refers to the seat of thinking and deciding. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

# Ecclesiastes 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter moves from wise conduct before a king to the injustice that Qoheleth observes, and it ends by affirming that no one can fully understand what God does.

1. The value of wisdom (1)
2. Wise conduct before a king (2–9)
    1. Obeying the king’s command (2–4)
    2. Knowing the right time and the limits of human power (5–9)
3. The wicked seem to escape judgment (10–14)
4. Commendation of joy (15)
5. The limits of understanding God’s work (16–17)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 8:1, 8:5–8, and 8:11–14.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The oath of God

In verse 2, Qoheleth grounds obedience to the king in an oath connected with God. This likely refers to a promise of loyalty to the king that people made in God’s name, though it could refer to God’s own oath concerning the king.

### Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears again in this chapter in verses 10 and 14. Render it consistently through the book.

### Fearing God

In verses 12 and 13, those who fear God are people who reverently acknowledge his rule and live accordingly. This is respectful submission, not terror.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Generic “him”

In several verses (6, 7, 15, and 17), “him” and “he” refer to people in general rather than to a specific person. If your language would not use a singular pronoun this way, you could use a plural or general expression.

### Textual variant in verse 10

Most Hebrew manuscripts say that the wicked were “forgotten” in the city, while some manuscripts and ancient versions say that they were “praised.” The ULT follows the second reading.

# Ecclesiastes 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter reflects on death as the one event that comes to every person, urges readers to enjoy life while they can, and ends with a story showing that wisdom is valuable even when people do not honor it.

  1. The same fate comes to everyone (1–3)
  2. The living have hope, but the dead are forgotten (4–6)
  3. A call to enjoy life and work with all your strength (7–10)
  4. Time and misfortune overtake all people (11–12)
  5. The value of wisdom (13–18)
    1. The poor wise man who delivered a city (13–15)
    2. Sayings about wisdom (16–18)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [9:2](../09/02.md), [9:4–6](../09/04.md), [9:11–12](../09/11.md), and [9:17–18](../09/17.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Sheol

In verse 10, [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hades]] is the place of the dead, where Qoheleth says there is no more work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom. Use a term that refers to the place where people go when they die, not a place of punishment.

### White clothes and oil

In verse 8, wearing white clothes and putting [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/oil]] on the head were signs of joy and celebration in the culture of that time. If your readers would not understand these as signs of joy, you could explain them in a footnote.

### Vapor

The Hebrew word rendered “vapor” is this book’s key term for what is fleeting and insubstantial, and it appears twice in verse 9. Render it consistently through the book.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “One happening”

In verses 2 and 3, the “one happening” that comes to everyone is death. Translate this in a way that makes clear that Qoheleth is speaking about the fate that all people share, whether they are righteous or wicked. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

Alternate translation: [I carefully considered]

# Ecclesiastes 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a collection of short wisdom sayings that contrast the wise person with the foolish person, especially in how each one acts, works, and speaks, and in how rulers govern.

1. A little folly ruins much wisdom (1–3)
2. Rulers and those under them (4–7)
    1. Stay calm when a ruler is angry (4)
    2. Rulers who give high positions to the wrong people (5–7)
3. Wisdom and the dangers of ordinary work (8–11)
4. The words of the wise and the words of fools (12–15)
5. Sayings about rulers, work, and speech (16–20)
    1. Foolish rulers and noble rulers (16–17)
    2. Laziness, feasting, and money (18–19)
    3. Do not curse the king even in private (20)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 10:1–20.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Right and left

In verse 2, the right side was associated with strength, protection, and favor, and the left side with weakness and misfortune. If your readers would not understand this association, you could express the meaning plainly or explain it in a footnote.

### Snake charming

In verse 11, the “master of the tongue” is a snake charmer, a person who used words or sounds to calm snakes so they would not bite. His skill is useless if the snake bites before he uses it.

### Feasting in the morning

In verse 16, princes who “eat in the morning” are feasting when they should be working, which showed that they did not take their responsibilities seriously.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Proverbs

Most verses in this chapter are proverbs that are only loosely connected to one another. Translate them in a way that sounds like a wise saying in your language, and keep each one short and memorable. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/writing-proverbs]])

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe **Flies** that are characterized by **death**. This could mean: (1) flies that have died Alternate translation: [Dead flies] or (2) flies that bring death or disease. Alternate translation: [Flies that bring death] If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way.

The point of this comparison is that just as **Flies of death** can spoil a whole container of **a perfumer’s oil**, so **a little foolishness** can spoil the good that **wisdom** and **honor** have accomplished. Qoheleth implies this comparison by placing the two statements next to each other. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in the same way, a little foolishness can spoil the good that wisdom or honor has accomplished]

Alternate translation: [the ruler becomes angry with you]

Qoheleth is using **do not leave your place** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not abandon your position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. # Ecclesiastes 11 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in all of chapter 11.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Advice

This chapter gives a series of disconnected pieces of advice. Translators should not try to smooth the transitions between these pieces of advice. The advice in these statements do not apply in every situation. Therefore, they should be seen as “good ideas.”

Quote: Send out your bread on the waters, for you will find it again after many days

# Ecclesiastes 12 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 12:1–7 and 12:13–14.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Advice

This chapter gives a series of disconnected pieces of advice. Translators should not try to smooth the transitions between these pieces of advice. The advice in these statements do not apply in every situation. Therefore, they should be seen as “good ideas.”

### Yahweh

At the end of a very impressive life, Solomon looks back and sees that the only real lasting thing in this world is Yahweh. The purpose of his life was to honor Yahweh, something he should have done far more throughout his life. Therefore, he felt that his life was wasted. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])
